analysis.one_liner: Restricts telemarketing calls, prerecorded auto-dialers, and junk faxes, and creates a national do-not-call list.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced by Sen. Larry Pressler with zero cosponsors, referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, and died there without a hearing or vote before the 102nd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have cracked down on unwanted telemarketing: it directed the Federal Communications Commission to set rules so that people could put their phone numbers on a national list that telemarketers would have to buy access to and avoid calling, at no charge to the person on the list. It would also have banned robot-dialed calls to emergency lines, hospital pagers, and cell phones, required junk faxes to identify the sender, and required prerecorded sales calls to state who was calling and hang up properly. The bill never got past its committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary phone subscribers, especially people at home who were getting sales calls they didn't want; the bill's own findings counted more than 300,000 solicitors calling more than 18 million Americans every day [S3]. Hospitals, fire and law enforcement agencies, and cell phone users would have gained from a ban on auto-dialed calls to emergency lines and mobile numbers [S3]. Fax recipients, who pay for paper and ink on junk faxes, would have gained from sender-identification and junk-fax restrictions [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residential phone subscribers and fax users

how_it_helps.text: Requires the FCC to set up a national do-not-call database of residential subscribers who object to solicitations, and makes it unlawful to call numbers on that list; subscribers cannot be charged to join or leave it [S3].
Bans auto-dialed unsolicited calls to emergency lines, hospital pagers, health care facilities, fire and law enforcement agencies, and to paging and cell phone numbers [S3].
Requires prerecorded sales messages to identify the business calling, give its number or address, and release the called party's line promptly after hang-up [S3].

Requires faxes and computer-sent junk faxes to carry the date and time, the sender's identity, and the sending machine's phone number, and directs the FCC to write rules restricting unsolicited fax advertisements [S3].
Leaves state laws that impose stricter rules untouched, so states could go further than the federal baseline [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Telemarketing companies — over 30,000 businesses generating $435 billion in 1990 sales, per the bill's findings — would bear the cost of screening numbers against the do-not-call list and buying access to it, and of new equipment and call-disclosure requirements [S3]. Fax machine makers would have to add identification-printing features within six months [S3]. Local phone carriers would have to notify subscribers of their opt-out right [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Telemarketing firms and fax equipment makers

drawbacks.text: The bill leaned on a national database that telemarketers would purchase by area code or exchange, a mechanism that costs money to administer and could shift costs into the prices of telemarketed goods and services [S3].

It directed the FCC to pick 'the most cost-effective' methods after a study rather than immediately imposing a hard ban, so the protections would have been delayed by a rulemaking of up to 240 days and would only take effect 30 days after rules were issued [S3].
It exempted tax-exempt nonprofit calls from the definition of telephone solicitation, so charitable and political-style solicitation calls would continue [S3].
Small telemarketing businesses were flagged as needing protection from unreasonable fee burdens, a sign that compliance costs fall hardest on smaller operators [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer benefits were broad and real — a workable do-not-call mechanism, safer emergency lines, and honest caller identification — while the costs fell on a large but concentrated industry and on equipment makers through modest technical requirements. The bill was built to balance: it let legitimate telemarketing continue while protecting privacy, and it preserved stricter state laws. Its main weakness was pacing, relying on an FCC study before rules took effect.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee on July 10, 1991, and sat there until the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993, never getting a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Larry Pressler (R-SD) introduced the Telephone Advertising Consumer Rights Act on July 10, 1991 [S1][S3].
No senators signed on as cosponsors [S4].
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S5].
The action history shows no further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — before the Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Telemarketing companies, which continued operating without any of the new federal call restrictions, fax rules, or do-not-call requirements the bill would have imposed; consumers who wanted relief from unwanted calls gained nothing from this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Telemarketing companies that faced no new restrictions

for.name: Sen. Larry Pressler
for.role: U.S. Senator from South Dakota; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to committee; it had no other Senate sponsors.

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on July 10, 1991 and took no further action on the bill for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill had no cosponsors, so there is no record of how parties lined up; the sole sponsor was a Republican.

industries.note: The bill would have forced telemarketers to screen out numbers on a national do-not-call list, buy access to that list, and disclose their identity on prerecorded calls, cutting into a $435 billion sales channel built on calls people did not ask for. Its interest ran directly against the phone subscribers the bill was protecting.

Makers would have had to add date/time, sender-identification, and phone-number printing to machines built after six months, a modest compliance cost. The requirement mainly served fax recipients, who otherwise pay for junk faxes out of their own paper and ink.
Carriers would have had to notify subscribers of their right to opt out of solicitations, an administrative duty with no revenue upside, but one that directly served their customers' privacy.
